Chapter 9: The Process of Change — From Fixing to Becoming
When you think about change, do you picture yourself fixing what’s broken? Most of us do. We spot our flaws, set ambitious goals, and push ourselves to work harder—hoping, one day, we’ll finally get it right.
But in person-centered therapy, change isn’t really about fixing. It’s about becoming. Imagine it as something that unfolds naturally—like letting your true self step forward, instead of forcing yourself into someone else’s mold.
Picture a man, tired after years of chasing self-improvement. He’s tried every trick, read every book, but somehow, he’s still stuck. When he comes to therapy, he’s looking for a brand-new strategy. But his therapist suggests something different—what if, instead of always trying to improve, he just focused on understanding and accepting himself, exactly as he is?
At first, that idea feels backwards. He’s used to measuring his worth by how much progress he’s made. But as he lets go of the urge to "fix" himself, something shifts. He starts treating his struggles with more compassion. He’s a little more patient with setbacks. And slowly, he realizes that real change doesn’t come from fighting himself—it comes from accepting himself.
Then there’s the college student, anxious about what’s next. Instead of chasing after grades or achievements, she learns to listen to her own experience. Her anxiety eases up when she stops trying to control every little outcome. She finds herself opening up to uncertainty—maybe even taking a few more risks.
The thing is, change in therapy isn’t fast or predictable. Sometimes you get a flash of insight, and sometimes you’re back in confusion or doubt. Old habits can creep in, and progress can feel hard to spot. But over time, people notice they’re handling challenges differently. They’re less reactive. They feel more grounded. Even in tough moments, they can stay present with themselves.
Here’s something most people miss: that urge to "fix" ourselves? It often comes from a deep place of self-rejection. In therapy, the invitation is to turn toward yourself with kindness. To trust that growth will happen, in its own time. The therapist’s acceptance is like a mirror—showing you how to accept yourself, flaws and all. That’s how you let go of perfectionism, and start embracing the messy, imperfect process of becoming.
Think of a woman who’s always felt inadequate. In therapy, she discovers she doesn’t have to earn her worth. She learns to appreciate her strengths and accept her limitations. And slowly, that constant pressure to be someone else fades away—replaced by a gentle sense of peace.
